user_query: Why does node2vec use a second-order random walk with parameters p and q instead of sampling the next node only according to the static edge weights w_vx?
llm_response: node2vec uses a second-order random walk because it wants the walk to be biased by the *previous step*, not just by the current node’s outgoing edge weights. The parameters p and q let it control the search behavior: p adjusts the likelihood of immediately revisiting the previous node, and q adjusts whether the walk behaves more like a breadth-first search (staying near the current neighborhood) or a depth-first search (moving outward to more distant nodes). This makes the sampled node sequences capture both local and more global graph structure, which a purely static, first-order walk based only on w_vx cannot do. In other words, w_vx alone encodes only edge strength from v to x, while node2vec’s second-order transition probability can depend on the edge (t, v) that brought the walk to v, allowing richer and more informative embeddings.
llm_confidence_reasoning: This is a standard and well-established description of node2vec’s biased second-order random walk and the roles of p and q.
